title: Compact Operators and Riesz Schauder Theory

items.title: Compact linear operator
items.strategy: Scaling proves the equivalence and compact sets are bounded, hence T is bounded. Require actual compact closure, not just precompactness in an incomplete target.
items.statement: For normed spaces X,Y over the same field R or C, a linear operator T is compact when every bounded set has image with compact closure in Y; equivalently the image of the closed unit ball has compact closure.
items.axiom_audit: No new choice is used beyond the explicitly declared supplier dependencies; any DC, AC_omega, or AC use is inherited along those dependency paths.

references.title: Theo Bühler and Dietmar Salamon, Functional Analysis — §4.2 p.183, Definition 4.20

items.title: Dependent choice implies countable choice
items.strategy: Finite histories: the one-term extension relation on finite partial choice functions is entire, DC produces a chain, and its union is a choice function on N. This is the local supplier replacing the later-page choice-implication theorem for DC-hypothesis consumers.
items.statement: In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice.
items.axiom_audit: The lemma is a ZF theorem relating two choice principles; DC is its hypothesis and no further choice is used.

references.title: H. Herrlich, Axiom of Choice, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1876 — finite-history proof that DC implies AC_omega

items.title: Sequential characterization of compact operators
items.strategy: Forward: decreasing closures of image tails inside a compact closure intersect. Pick a cluster point once and choose successive least eligible indices in shrinking balls; this direction needs no recursive arbitrary choices. Converse: use DC to select a separated image sequence if total boundedness fails, and to approximate a Cauchy sequence in the closure by image points; sequential hypothesis gives completeness of the closure, hence metric compactness.
items.statement: Assume DC. Then T:X->Y is compact iff every bounded sequence (x_n) has a subsequence for which T x_n converges in Y.
items.axiom_audit: The DC => AC_omega instance needed by the metric-compactness equivalence is supplied locally by lem-dependent-choice-implies-countable-choice; DC itself selects the separated sequence when total boundedness fails and the successive approximants to points of the image closure. The forward implication is ZF.

references.title: Theo Bühler and Dietmar Salamon, Functional Analysis — §4.2 p.183, Lemma 4.19

items.title: Bounded finite rank operators are compact
items.strategy: Its image of the unit ball is bounded inside a finite-dimensional range; closure there is compact and the finite-dimensional range is closed in the ambient normed target.
items.statement: A bounded finite-rank operator between normed spaces is compact.
items.axiom_audit: No new choice is used beyond the explicitly declared supplier dependencies; any DC, AC_omega, or AC use is inherited along those dependency paths.

items.title: Compositions with a compact operator are compact
items.strategy: A sends bounded sets to bounded sets; B maps compact closures continuously to compact sets.
items.statement: If T:X->Y is compact and A:W->X, B:Y->Z are bounded linear, then TA and BT are compact.
items.axiom_audit: No new choice is used beyond the explicitly declared supplier dependencies; any DC, AC_omega, or AC use is inherited along those dependency paths.

items.title: Linear combinations of compact operators are compact
items.statement: Compact operators X->Y form a linear subspace. Consequently any polynomial in a compact endomorphism with zero constant coefficient is compact.
items.strategy: For sums, use the continuous addition map on the product of the two compact image closures; scalar multiples are immediate. For polynomials apply the ideal property finitely many times.

items.title: Norm limit of compact operators is compact
items.strategy: For epsilon choose one T_n within epsilon/3. A finite epsilon/3 net for its unit-ball image gives a finite epsilon net for T. The closure is complete as closed in Banach Y, so it is compact by metric completeness and total boundedness.
items.statement: Assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice, if Y is Banach and compact operators T_n:X->Y converge in operator norm to T, then T is compact.
items.axiom_audit: Uses AC_omega exactly through the complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact supplier after constructing finite nets; no DC or full AC is used.

items.title: Approximable operator
items.strategy: Define the closure and apply norm-closedness of compact operators. Keep approximation-property distinctions for the B remark and FA-11.
items.statement: An approximable operator is in the operator-norm closure of bounded finite-rank operators. Assuming the Axiom of Countable Choice, an approximable operator with Banach target is compact; equality with all compact maps is not asserted in general.
items.axiom_audit: The closure definition is ZF. The compactness consequence uses AC_omega exactly through norm-closedness of the compact operators.
items.source_obligation: See batch coverage and notes; this local application or addition needs exact source support verified before readiness.

items.title: Schauder compact adjoint theorem
items.strategy: For compact T choose a finite delta net in T(B_X). Bounded functionals are determined up to norm epsilon on that image by their finitely many values: cover the bounded finite coordinate set and choose representatives in B_Y*. This gives total boundedness of T*(B_Y*); completeness of X* gives compactness. Apply this direction to T* for the converse and use T** J_X=J_Y T and the closed isometric image J_Y(Y). Banach transpose uses linear evaluation, no conjugation.
items.statement: Assume AC. For Banach spaces X,Y and bounded T:X->Y, T is compact iff its Banach transpose T*:Y*->X* is compact.
items.axiom_audit: AC is declared because the canonical-bidual isometry uses Hahn–Banach norming functionals and the converse closes the isometric copy J_Y(Y). DC is inherited from the selected metric-compactness route. The Banach-target hypothesis is indispensable.

references.title: Theo Bühler and Dietmar Salamon, Functional Analysis — §4.2 pp.186–187, Theorem 4.28(iii)

items.title: Compact operator sends weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent sequences
items.strategy: Uniform boundedness applied to J_X x_n gives norm boundedness. If norm convergence fails take a bad subsequence, then a compact image subsequence. Each functional identifies its norm limit with Tx because transpose preserves weak convergence and the dual separates points.
items.statement: Assume AC. For Banach X,Y, compact T and x_n weakly converging to x, ||T x_n-Tx|| ->0.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC supplies Hahn--Banach separation (cor-dual-separates-points, the canonical bidual isometry) and, through lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration, the DC used by uniform boundedness and sequential compactness.

items.title: Kernel of identity minus compact is finite dimensional
items.strategy: The kernel is closed; its unit ball is closed in the compact closure of K(B_X), since K is the identity there. Apply the finite-dimensional compact-ball characterization.
items.statement: For compact K:X->X on a normed space, ker(I-K) is finite dimensional.
items.axiom_audit: No new choice is used beyond the explicitly declared supplier dependencies; any DC, AC_omega, or AC use is inherited along those dependency paths.

items.title: Range of identity minus compact is closed
items.strategy: If the estimate fails, select quotient-normalized representatives x_n with dist(x_n,N)=1, ||x_n||<=2, and (I-K)x_n ->0. Compactness gives a convergent subsequence of Kx_n and hence x_n; its limit is in N, contradiction. Apply the earlier quotient-estimate criterion.
items.statement: Assume DC. For compact K on Banach X, ran(I-K) is closed and dist(x,ker(I-K)) <= C||(I-K)x|| for some C.
items.axiom_audit: DC is used to select the quotient-normalized contradiction sequence and is also the exact hypothesis of the closed-range quotient estimate.
items.source_obligation: See batch coverage and notes; this local application or addition needs exact source support verified before readiness.

items.title: Riesz schauder ascent and descent stabilize
items.strategy: A^n=I-K_n with compact K_n, so preceding kernel/range lemmas apply. If kernel chain strictly grows, Riesz-separated unit vectors have K-images separated modulo earlier kernels. For descending closed ranges choose x_n in ran(A^n) at distance >1/2 from ran(A^(n+1)); for m>n, Kx_m and Ax_n lie in ran(A^(n+1)), again separating Kx_n. DC gives contradictions to compactness. Stability implies direct sum algebraically by writing A^m x=A^(2m)y. Bounded inverse applies on the closed stable range. No index theorem is used here.
items.statement: Assume DC. For A=I-K with K compact on Banach X, both ker(A^n) and ran(A^n) stabilize. For sufficiently large m, X=ker(A^m) direct-sum ran(A^m), with finite-dimensional kernel and closed range; A restricts to a bounded isomorphism on ran(A^m).
items.axiom_audit: DC for separated selections; no forward use of index zero.

items.title: Fredholm alternative for identity minus compact
items.strategy: On the stabilized decomposition, A is invertible on the range summand and nilpotent on its finite-dimensional kernel summand; rank-nullity gives equality of defect dimensions and injectivity/surjectivity equivalence. Since ran A is closed, the elementary annihilator identity gives the stated solvability condition.
items.statement: Assume AC. For compact K on Banach X over a fixed F=R or C, I-K is injective iff surjective, then boundedly invertible. For general y, (I-K)x=y is solvable iff phi(y)=0 for every phi in ker(I-K*). The kernel and cokernel are finite dimensional of equal dimension over F.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC supplies Hahn--Banach annihilator separation, and through lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration the DC used by stabilization and bounded inversion.

items.title: Neumann series and small perturbations of bounded inverses
items.statement: For Banach X and ||R||<1, (I-R)^(-1)=sum_{n>=0}R^n in operator norm. If A:X->Y is boundedly invertible and ||A^(-1)E||<1, then A+E is boundedly invertible.
items.strategy: Use completeness of bounded-operator space and geometric norm estimates. Multiply partial sums on both sides and pass to limits. Factor A+E=A(I+A^(-1)E). This is the operator-only precursor to the later Banach-algebra lemma.
items.axiom_audit: No new choice is used beyond the explicitly declared supplier dependencies; any DC, AC_omega, or AC use is inherited along those dependency paths.

items.title: Spectrum and resolvent of a bounded operator
items.statement: For bounded T on a complex Banach space X, rho(T)={lambda in C:lambda I-T has a bounded two-sided inverse}; sigma(T)=C minus rho(T).
items.strategy: Define eigenvalues, eigenspaces, and generalized eigenspace union_n ker(T-lambda I)^n; algebraic multiplicity is its dimension when finite and lambda is an eigenvalue. The real-operator complexification convention belongs to later FA-17. No Banach algebra or general spectral nonemptiness theorem is presumed.
items.axiom_audit: No new choice is used beyond the explicitly declared supplier dependencies; any DC, AC_omega, or AC use is inherited along those dependency paths.

items.title: Riesz schauder spectrum of a compact operator
items.strategy: Scale I-K/lambda for the Fredholm alternative and stabilization. The generalized kernel is finite dimensional. On the stable closed range K-lambda I is invertible and remains so nearby by Neumann perturbation; on the finite-dimensional nilpotent block only lambda is spectral, as its finite geometric inverse shows. Neumann gives an open resolvent and excludes |lambda|>||K||. Thus spectrum intersect {|lambda|>=epsilon} is compact in C=R^2 by Heine–Borel and every one of its points is isolated. Its singleton cover has a finite subcover, proving finiteness. For 0 on infinite-dimensional X, a bounded inverse would make I compact by the ideal property. No general spectral nonemptiness theorem or forward functional calculus is used.
items.statement: Assume AC. For compact K on complex Banach X, every nonzero spectral value is an isolated eigenvalue with finite algebraic multiplicity; for each epsilon>0 only finitely many spectral values satisfy |lambda|>=epsilon. If X is infinite dimensional, 0 is spectral.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC is declared directly for the Fredholm alternative and annihilator separation; lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration supplies the DC stabilization chain. No claim says that zero is an eigenvalue or isolated; finite-dimensional zero may be resolvent.

items.title: Spectrum of a compact operator is countable with only zero as possible accumulation
items.strategy: Cover nonzero spectrum by the finite sets {|lambda|>=1/n}. State the countable-union choice cost conservatively; subset of C could also be enumerated geometrically.
items.statement: Assume AC. The spectrum of a compact operator on complex Banach X is countable, and its only possible accumulation point is zero.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC is propagated from the compact-spectrum theorem and in particular supplies the AC_omega used to enumerate the countable union of finite annular pieces.

items.title: Fredholm operator cokernel and index
items.strategy: Distinguish algebraic cokernel from its quotient topology; closed range is explicitly part of the definition.
items.statement: A bounded T:X->Y between Banach spaces is Fredholm if ker T is finite dimensional, ran T is closed, and coker T=Y/ran T is finite dimensional; ind T=dim ker T-dim coker T.
items.axiom_audit: No new choice is used beyond the explicitly declared supplier dependencies; any DC, AC_omega, or AC use is inherited along those dependency paths.

items.title: Fredholm splitting and parametrix
items.strategy: Use complemented finite-dimensional kernel and closed finite-codimensional range. T:X_1->ran T is boundedly invertible. Define S as this inverse on ran T and zero on Y_0, and identify defects as minus the finite-rank projections.
items.statement: Assume AC. For Fredholm T:X->Y there are bounded decompositions X=ker T direct-sum X_1 and Y=ran T direct-sum Y_0 and bounded S:Y->X with ST-I_X and TS-I_Y finite rank.
items.axiom_audit: AC is explicit because the complemented-kernel and complemented-range suppliers use Hahn–Banach extensions to obtain bounded complements. The bounded inverse step inherits DC.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis, version November 17, 2017 — §6.5 p.186, equations (6.65)–(6.67)

items.title: A compact remainder estimate forces closed range
items.statement: Assume DC. Suppose T:X->Y is bounded between Banach spaces and ||x||<=C||Tx||+||Kx|| for a compact K:X->Z with Banach Z. Then ker T is finite dimensional and ran T is closed.
items.strategy: On ker T the estimate and compact subsequences imply unit-ball compactness. For closed range repeat the normalized quotient representatives argument: if dist(x,ker T)<=Cprime||Tx|| fails, select ||x_n||<=2, dist=1, Tx_n->0. A convergent Kx_n subsequence and the estimate on differences force x_n Cauchy; its limit contradicts dist=1. Invoke quotient-estimate criterion.
items.axiom_audit: DC via normalized representatives and compact subsequences; no Fredholm index assumption.

references.title: Theo Bühler and Dietmar Salamon, Functional Analysis — §4.3 pp.193–194, Lemma 4.39

items.title: Atkinson
items.strategy: Fredholm=>S is the preceding splitting construction. Conversely choose a bound b for the bounded operator S; then ||x||<=b||Tx||+||(I-ST)x|| gives finite kernel and closed range by the compact-remainder lemma. Apply Schauder to I_Y-TS: its transpose I_{Y*}-S*T* is compact. Thus ker T* is contained in ker(S*T*)=ker(I_{Y*}-(I_{Y*}-S*T*)), which is finite dimensional by the identity-minus-compact kernel lemma. The dual of Y/ran T is ker T*; dual norming implies a normed space with finite-dimensional dual is finite dimensional (embed by a dual basis), proving finite cokernel. The later Calkin equivalence is orientation only and supplies nothing here.
items.statement: Assume AC. For bounded T:X->Y between Banach spaces, T is Fredholm iff some bounded S:Y->X satisfies ST-I_X and TS-I_Y compact.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC is declared directly for splitting, Schauder, and Hahn--Banach dual norming; lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration supplies the DC compact-remainder lemma.

items.title: Fredholm index is additive
items.strategy: Compose parametrices; compact ideal and sum properties give Fredholmness by Atkinson. Verify the exact sequence 0 -> ker T -> ker UT -> ker U -> coker T -> coker UT -> coker U ->0, where maps are T, quotient, U on cosets, quotient. Every term is finite dimensional. Rank-nullity telescopes dimensions.
items.statement: Assume AC. For Fredholm T:X->Y and U:Y->Z, UT is Fredholm and ind(UT)=ind U+ind T.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC is propagated from Atkinson's theorem; the finite exact-sequence dimension calculation adds no further choice.

items.title: Fredholm index is locally constant
items.strategy: Use the Fredholm splitting. For a sufficiently small perturbation, the block from X_1 to ran T remains invertible by Neumann. Bounded invertible row/column operations reduce the map to that block plus its finite-dimensional Schur complement ker T -> Y_0. This gives closed range and finite defects, with index dim ker T-dim Y_0 regardless of the Schur complement rank.
items.statement: Assume AC. Fredholm operators form an open subset of B(X,Y), and their integer index is locally constant in operator norm.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC is propagated from the Fredholm splitting; the finite-dimensional Schur-complement rank calculation adds no further choice.

items.title: Fredholm index is stable under compact perturbations
items.strategy: A parametrix for T is a parametrix modulo compact maps for every T+tK, t in [0,1]. Atkinson gives Fredholmness along the path, local constancy and connectedness of the interval give index equality.
items.statement: Assume AC. If T:X->Y is Fredholm and K:X->Y is compact, then T+K is Fredholm with ind(T+K)=ind T.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC is propagated from Atkinson and local constancy; connectedness of the parameter interval adds no choice.

items.title: Lambda identity minus compact has index zero
items.strategy: Apply compact perturbation invariance to invertible lambda I, whose kernel and cokernel vanish. This is a later index restatement; the earlier Fredholm alternative did not use it.
items.statement: Assume AC. For compact K on Banach X and nonzero scalar lambda, lambda I-K is Fredholm of index zero.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC is propagated from compact-perturbation invariance; the index computation for the scalar identity is finite-dimensional and adds no choice.

title: Compact Operators and Riesz Schauder Theory — Examples

items.title: Diagonal operator on ell p is compact iff diagonal tends to zero
items.strategy: First use the counting-measure proposition to make (N,P(N),#) a measure space and the ell-p/counting-measure remark to identify its real Lp quotient isometrically with the usual real sequence space; Riesz-Fischer completeness of Lp therefore transfers to real ell-p. For complex scalars, take real and imaginary parts of a Cauchy sequence, use that real and imaginary parts are norm contractions, and recombine their real ell-p limits; the triangle inequality gives complex norm convergence. Truncations have finite rank and operator-norm error sup_{n>N}|a_n|. Conversely nonvanishing tail gives infinitely many separated D_a e_n, contradicting compactness. This covers p=infinity without falsely calling e_n a Schauder basis there.
items.statement: Assume DC. For 1<=p<=infinity and a function a:N->K bounded in modulus, D_a on ell^p(N), identified with counting-measure L^p(N), is compact iff for every epsilon>0 the tail satisfies |a_n|<epsilon.
items.axiom_audit: DC is used by the sequential characterization converse; lem-dependent-choice-implies-countable-choice supplies the AC_omega assumptions of the norm-closure and Lp-completeness suppliers.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis, version November 17, 2017 — §3.1 p.70, example after Theorem 3.2

items.title: Continuous kernel integral operator is compact on c of an interval
items.strategy: Continuous-integrability makes K well defined. Heine--Cantor and the uniform integral bound give boundedness of the image unit ball and the componentwise modulus estimate 2(b-a)sup_y|k(x,y)-k(xprime,y)|. Apply the published real compact-metric Ascoli theorem. For complex functions prove the same integral estimates by real/imaginary parts and apply Ascoli to those two parts, then choose a nested subsequence and approximate sequences in the closure using Countable Choice.
items.statement: Assume DC. For a<b and continuous real- or complex-valued k on [a,b]^2, Kf(x)=integral_a^b k(x,y)f(y)dy is compact on C([a,b]) over the same scalar field, with its supremum norm.
items.axiom_audit: DC, and AC_omega through the locally proved lem-dependent-choice-implies-countable-choice, are used exactly by the published Arzela--Ascoli subsequence corollary and the metric-compactness equivalence; the integration and real/imaginary-part reductions are ZF.

items.title: Identity is compact iff the space is finite dimensional
items.strategy: Apply the earlier closed-unit-ball characterization directly; on ell^2 this gives the standard noncompact identity.
items.statement: The identity of a normed space is compact iff the space is finite dimensional.

items.strategy: Bound P by one and identify its one-dimensional range. Coordinate e_2 is outside the closed range.

items.title: Fredholm alternative for an integral equation
items.strategy: Use the same-page compact-kernel example and the abstract Fredholm alternative. Keep the Banach transpose in C([a,b])*; do not identify it with a conjugated L^2 kernel without additional measure duality. The interval is the concrete compact K; no PDE claim.
items.statement: Assume AC. For a continuous kernel on a compact interval, f-Kf=g in C([a,b]) is solvable exactly when every phi in ker(I-K*) annihilates g; uniqueness for all g is equivalent to a trivial homogeneous kernel.
items.axiom_audit: Full AC is declared directly for the abstract Fredholm alternative, and lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration supplies the weaker DC and AC_omega assumptions used by the continuous-kernel Ascoli example.

items.title: Compactness is not preserved by strong operator limits
items.strategy: Define strong convergence here as convergence P_N x -> x for each x. Square-summable tails give this; test e_(N+1) for norm error. Use the A compact-ball criterion directly instead of a cross-page B dependency.
items.statement: On ell^2, coordinate projections P_N have finite rank and converge strongly to I, but I is not compact and ||I-P_N||=1.
items.axiom_audit: No new choice is used beyond the explicitly declared supplier dependencies; any DC, AC_omega, or AC use is inherited along those dependency paths.

items.title: Approximation property controls finite rank density in compact operators
items.strategy: For compact closure C=T(B_X), use AP to choose finite-rank R:Y->Y uniformly epsilon-close to identity on C; RT is finite rank and ||RT-T||<=epsilon. Connect to FA-11 AP/BAP definitions. Do not infer from failure of AP alone a particular unproved counterexample on Y->Y. The converse all-domain characterization needs separate proof and is not silently asserted.
items.statement: If Banach Y has the approximation property, every compact T:X->Y is approximable. This is not a universal finite-rank approximation theorem for arbitrary Banach targets.
items.axiom_audit: Literature-derived remark proof not-applicable; explicit explanatory argument remains reviewable.

items.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operator and Hilbert–Schmidt norm
items.statement: Let H,K be real or complex Hilbert spaces, E a Hilbert basis of H, and T in B(H,K) bounded. The Hilbert–Schmidt square-sum is s_E(T):=Σ_{e∈E}||Te||², the supremum of the finite subsums over the finite subsets of E; T is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to E when s_E(T)<+∞, and then ||T||_{HS,E}:=s_E(T)^{1/2}. The definition is choice-free, keeps E in the notation, makes no basis-existence or operator-norm claim, and records the degenerate cases H={0}, zero operator and finite E.
items.strategy: Introduce the finite-subset-supremum convention explicitly, including the zero, finite-dimensional, and unbounded-supremum cases. Do not append a basis-extension or operator-norm claim to this choice-free definition.
items.axiom_audit: ZF: the Hilbert basis is supplied as data; no basis existence claim, no selection, no comparison with the operator norm.

items.title: The Hilbert–Schmidt norm is basis independent
items.statement: Assume AC_ω. For bounded T:H→K and Hilbert bases E of H, F of K, the rectangle supremum sup_{A⊆E,B⊆F finite}Σ|⟨Te,f⟩|² equals Σ_{e∈E}||Te||² and Σ_{f∈F}||T*f||²; hence the square-sum is independent of the Hilbert basis of H and equals the adjoint square-sum, and Hilbert–Schmidt membership and the relative norm are basis independent.
items.strategy: Apply Parseval to each Te, but never replace an arbitrary-index sum by an enumeration. Show both iterated finite-subset suprema equal the supremum over finite rectangles A×B: for a fixed finite A, finite choice permits combining the finitely many approximating B_e into one finite B, and then interchange A and B. Use ⟨Te,f⟩=⟨e,T*f⟩ with the page's first-variable-linear convention, and apply Parseval in the other direction.
items.axiom_audit: AC_ω is used exactly through the two Parseval instances (basis F applied to each Te, basis E applied to each T*f); the finite-subset bookkeeping uses only finite choice and the adjoint identity ⟨Te,f⟩=⟨e,T*f⟩.

references.title: John Roe, Lectures on Analysis — Lecture 13, Definition 13.1 and the preceding matrix-coefficient calculation, printed p. 67
Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis — §3.6, Lemma 3.23, printed pp. 93–94

items.title: Hilbert–Schmidt operators are compact
items.statement: Assume AC_ω. If E is a Hilbert basis of H and s_E(T)<+∞, then T is compact; moreover ||T−TP_F||≤(Σ_{e∈E\F}||Te||²)^{1/2} for every finite F⊆E, the truncations TP_F are compact finite-rank pieces, and a sequence of tail-control sets puts T in the norm closure of the compact operators of the Hilbert (hence Banach) target.
items.strategy: Choose F so that the finite-subset-supremum tail is small. Fourier expansion gives x=lim_G Σ_{e∈G}⟨x,e⟩e; boundedness of T, not an orthogonality claim about the vectors Te, passes this net through T. On each finite tail sum, the triangle inequality followed by scalar Cauchy–Schwarz gives ||Σ⟨x,e⟩Te||≤(Σ|⟨x,e⟩|^2)^{1/2}(Σ||Te||^2)^{1/2}; Parseval bounds the first factor by ||x||. Each TP_F has finite rank, and AC_omega norm-closure applies because K is Hilbert.
items.axiom_audit: AC_ω is used exactly for the Fourier expansion net of x, for the AC_ω norm-closure theorem applied to the sequence TP_{F_n}, and to select the tail-control sets F_n (countable choice). No enumeration of E is used.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis — §3.6, Lemma 3.23, printed pp. 93–94
John Roe, Lectures on Analysis — Lecture 13, Exercise 13.4 after Proposition 13.3, printed p. 68

items.title: Product rectangle kernels are dense in product L two
items.statement: Assume AC_ω. For sigma-finite (X,μ),(Y,ν), finite complex linear combinations of rectangle kernels 1_A(x)1_B(y) with μ(A),ν(B)<+∞ are dense in L²(μ×ν;C) and in L² of the completed product.
items.strategy: Choose increasing finite-measure exhaustions X_n,Y_n. Truncate k to X_n×Y_n and use Tonelli/continuity from below to make the L2 tail small. On this finite product, first replace a completion-measurable representative by a base-measurable one and approximate it by a finite complex simple function. Prove locally that sets approximable in symmetric-difference measure by the finite-rectangle algebra form a sigma-algebra: complements preserve error, while for a countable union continuity from below reduces to a finite union and countable subadditivity controls the accumulated error. The generating-algebra lemma therefore approximates every simple-function level set. Indicator L2 error is the square root of symmetric-difference measure. Extend the resulting finite rectangle combination by zero; every side has finite measure.
items.axiom_audit: AC_ω is used exactly by the completion-representative theorem when passing from the completed product to product-measurable level sets. The finite-measure exhaustion, the trace algebra/generation argument, the generating-algebra approximation and the density-of-simple-functions input are choice-free.

references.title: Sheldon Axler, Measure, Integration & Real Analysis — product measure and Lp approximation ingredients, §§7A, 10C
Published local finite-measure rectangle-density proof, sourced to Axler 10.70 and a generating-algebra argument

items.title: L two kernels give Hilbert–Schmidt operators
items.statement: Assume AC. For sigma-finite (X,μ),(Y,ν) and k in L² of the completed product: a product-measurable representative k_0 of the same norm exists; the section integral (T_kf)(x)=∫k_0(x,y)f(y)dν(y) is defined for μ-a.e. x, independent of representatives, measurable, and T_k:L²(ν;C)→L²(μ;C) is bounded with ||T_k||≤||k||₂; for every Hilbert bases E of L²(ν;C) and F of L²(μ;C), Σ_{e∈E}||T_ke||²=Σ_{f∈F}||T_k^*f||²=||k||₂², so T_k is Hilbert–Schmidt with ||T_k||_HS=||k||₂.
items.strategy: Pass to a base-measurable representative with equal norm (monotone convergence for the comparison of the completed and product integrals), prove the a.e. section integral with its Cauchy–Schwarz bound and measurability by simple-function approximation, exhibit Hilbert bases by Zorn with the orthogonal decomposition, form the orthonormal product family of the two bases, show rectangle kernels lie in its closed span via the Fourier nets, put k in that span by rectangle density, and use Bessel with a finite-Parseval lower bound for the exact value; transfer to the basis sums by Parseval and identify the adjoint sum by ⟨Te,f⟩=⟨e,T*f⟩. Every well-definedness, sigma-finite and representative reduction used is proved inside the item.
items.axiom_audit: AC is declared and used exactly to obtain/extend Hilbert bases by Zorn’s lemma (with the orthogonal decomposition for maximality); the published bridge lemma supplies the AC_ω used by the completion-representative theorem, Parseval/Fourier expansion, the Hilbert structure of L² and Riesz representation for T_k^*. The product-family, density and boundedness computations use no further choice.

references.title: John Roe, Lectures on Analysis — Lecture 13, Proposition 13.5, printed pp. 67–68
Gerald Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis — §3.6, Lemma 3.23 and matrix-coefficient characterization, printed pp. 93–95

title: Square-Integrable Kernels and Hilbert–Schmidt Compactness: Examples

items.title: A square-integrable separable product kernel
items.statement: Assume AC. For sigma-finite (X,μ),(Y,ν), a∈L²(μ;C), b∈L²(ν;C), the kernel k(x,y)=a(x)overline{b(y)} is square integrable of norm ||a||₂||b||₂, T_kf=a⟨f,b⟩, the range lies in the space of dimension at most one C·a (ordered basis of length at most one), and ||T_k||=||T_k||_HS=||a||₂||b||₂, with the zero cases a=0 and b=0 included.
items.strategy: Use Tonelli to factor ||k||_2^2, observe the first-variable-linear inner-product convention in the integral, and invoke the kernel theorem for the exact Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Treat a=0 or b=0 explicitly.
items.axiom_audit: AC is declared and propagated from the kernel theorem (its AC_ω consequences are supplied by the published bridge lemma); the product-kernel factorization and norm computations are otherwise choice-free.
items.source_obligation: Supported by the product-kernel calculation in the batch's Teschl/Roe treatments and fully derived from the A-page theorem.

items.title: A square-integrable kernel without a continuous representative
items.statement: Assume AC. On [0,1]² with the completed product of the two factor Lebesgue measures, the kernel k(x,y)=1_{[0,1/2]}(x) is square integrable of norm squared 1/2 with rank-one operator (the formula is an identity of L² classes) T_kf=⟨f,1_{[0,1]}⟩1_{[0,1/2]}, and its L² class has no continuous representative: no continuous h on the square agrees with k almost everywhere.
items.strategy: The product example proves square-integrability and rank one. If a continuous h agreed with k a.e., continuity plus positivity of every nonempty open rectangle forces h=1 on (0,1/2)×(0,1) and h=0 on (1/2,1)×(0,1), contradicting continuity along x=1/2. Handle boundary/null-set conventions explicitly.
items.axiom_audit: AC is declared; Countable Choice is used exactly to select one point outside the null disagreement set in each of countably many balls. The positivity of boxes, the propagation of values along sequences and the interface contradiction are choice-free.
items.source_obligation: A local counterexample separating L2 kernels from the earlier continuous-kernel example; its complete proof is contained in the strategy.

items.title: Finite-rank truncations of a square-integrable kernel
items.statement: Assume AC. On N×N with counting measure, for a=(a_n)∈ℓ² the diagonal kernel k(m,n)=a_n δ_{mn} is square integrable of norm ||a||₂ and T_k is the diagonal map (T_kf)(m)=a_mf(m); the truncations k_N have finite rank (explicit ordered basis of standard vectors), are compact, and satisfy ||T_k−T_{k_N}||_HS=(Σ_{n>N}|a_n|²)^{1/2} and ||T_k−T_{k_N}||=sup_{n>N}|a_n|.
items.strategy: Use the counting-measure dictionary and Tonelli to identify the square integral with the coefficient sum, verify sigma-finiteness by the exhaustion N=∪_{N}{0,…,N}, compute the diagonal action coordinatewise, exhibit the explicit ordered basis of the truncation ranges, and test standard basis vectors for the lower operator-norm bound with the pointwise diagonal estimate for the upper bound; the exact Hilbert–Schmidt error is the kernel theorem applied to the difference kernel.
items.axiom_audit: AC is declared and propagates to the kernel theorem and the Hilbert–Schmidt compactness theorem through the published bridge lemma; the counting-measure dictionary, the explicit truncation bases and the two exact error computations use no further choice.
items.source_obligation: Teschl §3.6 treats diagonal Hilbert–Schmidt operators; the exact truncation errors are computed locally.

items.title: A Hilbert–Schmidt kernel operator is compact on L two
items.statement: Assume AC. For sigma-finite (X,μ),(Y,ν) and k∈L² of the completed product, the kernel operator T_k:L²(ν;C)→L²(μ;C) is compact; in particular the discontinuous kernel of the preceding example is compact, so compactness of the integral operator does not require continuity of the kernel.
items.strategy: The kernel theorem supplies well-definedness and a Hilbert basis whose square-sum is finite, so T_k is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to it; the Hilbert–Schmidt compactness theorem then gives compactness. The preceding discontinuous kernel is recorded as the witness that continuity of the kernel is not needed.
items.axiom_audit: AC is declared; AC_ω (from the published bridge lemma) is used exactly by the Hilbert–Schmidt compactness theorem applied to T_k relative to a Hilbert basis of L²(ν;C) whose square-sum equals ||k||₂² by the kernel theorem.

references.title: John Roe, Lectures on Analysis — Proposition 13.5 and Exercise 13.4, printed p. 68
